newsitem.title: FRANCE: Credit Lyonnais workers take pay cut to save jobs.
newsitem.headline: Credit Lyonnais workers take pay cut to save jobs.

text.p: Employees of French bank Credit Lyonnais have voted to take home smaller pay cheques to save 1,000 jobs out of 5,000 slated to be axed, the state-controlled bank said on Friday.
The 82 percent vote in favour of the pay reduction by the 34,000 employees was believed to be the first time such a large enterprise in France had put its workforce to such a severe test.
"We see this as a success," said a spokeswoman for the bank, which has been digging out from a lending spree that almost brought its collapse in the early 1990s.
"Saving 1,000 jobs is pretty good news. This is an old bank and there is a sense of team spirit," she said.
As a result of the vote, some 7,000 back office support employees will see their work week cut to 33 hours from 39.

But with the so-called "solidarity contribution" from their fellow employees and provisions of a job-saving measure known as the Robien Law passed last year by the centre-right government, they will be paid for 37 hours.
The "solidarity contribution" amounting to 0.6 percent of employees' gross annual wages was part of an agreement last December between Credit Lyonnais and the unions.

The bank is cutting jobs as part of a drive to reduce costs to boost its profitability and prepare for privatisation after running up losses of 21 billion francs ($3.6 billion) between 1992 and 1994 from its expansion binge.
Those employees who voted against the wage cut will not have their pay cheques docked but those who accepted the proposal will get three extra days holiday.
The Robien Law, named after its sponsor, centre-right politician Gilles de Robien, gives employers relief on social security payroll charges when they reduce working hours to save jobs.
The government has said that the law has proved so popular among companies it may have to be changed to make it less generous.

Credit Lyonnais edged back into the black in 1995 with a profit of 13 million, helped by massive amounts of state aid. It had a 1996 profit of 202 million francs and a vastly improved underlying performance, reflecting in part the benefits of its cost cutting drive.
The government has said it hopes to privatise the bank in late 1998 or early 1999.
-- Penny MacRae, Paris Newsroom +33 1 4221 5452 ($ = 5.809 French Francs)
